body: Security and correctness problem: a client-supplied negative cursor offset (e.g. `cursor=0:-100:0`) gets passed straight into `queryset[start_offset:stop]`. The comment says this allows "access to data beyond normal pagination bounds", which is not something a paginator should ever do. Also, Django querysets don't support negative indexing and raise `ValueError: Negative indexing is not supported`, so a user can trigger a 500 at will. Clamp the offset to >= 0 (or reject negative offsets) whatever the flag says.

`OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key` runs `math.floor`/`math.ceil` directly on the attribute. The audit log endpoint uses `order_by="-datetime"`, so the value is a `datetime` and this raises `TypeError` as soon as any result is returned. `value_from_cursor` has the matching problem: it returns the raw int cursor value, which `build_queryset` then compares against a datetime column. Both need the DateTimePaginator conversion (epoch * multiplier and back). The simplest fix is to subclass DateTimePaginator.

This change to BasePaginator affects every paginator in the codebase. For `is_prev` cursors a negative offset now goes unclamped into the queryset slice, and Django raises on negative indexing, so any endpoint returns a 500 for a crafted `cursor=x:-1:1`. The comment "the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions" is wrong. Keep the clamp for both directions (`max(0, offset)`). Separately, the later `len(results) == offset + limit + extra` check still uses `offset` instead of `start_offset`.

`organization_context.member` can be `None`, for example for staff or superuser-in-non-active-mode users who aren't org members. A non-superuser with no membership then gets an `AttributeError`. Separately, `request.user.is_superuser` checks the raw flag and not whether superuser mode is active (`is_active_superuser(request)`), which bypasses the usual superuser sudo checks. Gating a paginator on a query param plus these permission checks also looks unnecessary.

Any admin who passes `optimized_pagination=true` now goes to `OptimizedCursorPaginator`, which is broken for this datetime-keyed queryset (TypeError in `get_item_key`, int-vs-datetime cursor comparison) and accepts negative offsets. This turns a feature flag in the query string into a crash path.

`zpopmin` silently drops the spans with the smallest end timestamps once a segment passes 1000. There is no metric or log, so the data loss is invisible; the old flush path at least emitted `segment_span_count_exceeded`. The limit is also hardcoded to 1000 and ignores `SpansBuffer.max_segment_spans` (default 1001), which is now unused. Pass the limit in as an ARGV and emit a metric when spans are evicted.

This lowers the redirect-depth limit from 10000 to 1000 and removes the comment explaining its effect. Segment trees deeper than 1000 will no longer be joined correctly, and they'll be split into separate segments. That change in behavior isn't mentioned or explained in the PR.

This removes the `max_segment_spans` check at flush time, so `max_segment_spans` is now dead config. It is also a behavior change: previously oversized segments were dropped and counted in metrics, and now they are truncated by the Lua script with no metric. Either keep the metric or wire the limit into the script. The module docstring also still describes the `span-buf:s:*` keys as sets, but they are now sorted sets.

`val["end_timestamp_precise"]` raises `KeyError` for any message missing the field, and that crashes the whole batch/consumer. If the field isn't guaranteed on every message (older producers, replayed backlog), use `.get()` with a fallback or skip the message. Also, `zadd` keys by payload, so two spans with byte-identical payloads collapse into one entry, the same as before with sets.
